  - paragraph:
    - text: Alan Mathison Turing (
    - link /ˈtjʊərɪŋ/:
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English
    - text: ; 23 June 1912 – 7 June 1954) was an English mathematician,
    - link "computer scientist":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_scientist
    - text: ","
    - link "logician":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic
    - text: ","
    - link "cryptanalyst":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalyst
    - text: ", philosopher and"
    - link "theoretical biologist":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_biologist
    - text: .
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-1-7"
    - text: He was highly influential in the development of
    - link "theoretical computer science":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_computer_science
    - text: ", providing a formalisation of the concepts of"
    - link "algorithm":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm
    - text: and
    - link "computation":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation
    - text: with the
    - link "Turing machine":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_machine
    - text: ", which can be considered a model of a general-purpose computer."
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-frs-8"
    - superscript:
      - link "[8]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-AFP-9"
    - superscript:
      - link "[9]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-2-10"
    - text: Turing is widely considered to be the father of theoretical computer science.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-3-11"
  - paragraph:
    - text: Born in London, Turing was raised in
    - link "southern England":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_England
    - text: . He graduated from
    - link "King's College, Cambridge":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge
    - text: ", and in 1938, earned a doctorate degree from"
    - link "Princeton University":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University
    - text: . During
    - link "World War II":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II
    - text: ", Turing worked for the"
    - link "Government Code and Cypher School":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Code_and_Cypher_School
    - text: at
    - link "Bletchley Park":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bletchley_Park
    - text: ", Britain's"
    - link "codebreaking":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codebreaking
    - text: centre that produced
    - link "Ultra":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_(cryptography)
    - text: intelligence. He led
    - link "Hut 8":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hut_8
    - text: ", the section responsible for German naval cryptanalysis. Turing devised techniques for speeding the breaking of German"
    - link "ciphers":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher
    - text: ", including improvements to the pre-war Polish"
    - link "bomba":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomba_(cryptography)
    - text: method, an
    - link "electromechanical":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromechanical
    - text: machine that could find settings for the
    - link "Enigma machine":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_machine
    - text: . He played a crucial role in cracking intercepted messages that enabled the
    - link "Allies":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_2
    - text: to defeat the
    - link "Axis powers":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers
    - text: in the
    - link "Battle of the Atlantic":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Atlantic
    - text: and other engagements.
    - superscript:
      - link "[11]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-bbc-copeland-12"
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-4-13"
  - paragraph:
    - text: After the war, Turing worked at the
    - link "National Physical Laboratory":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Physical_Laboratory_(United_Kingdom)
    - text: ", where he designed the"
    - link "Automatic Computing Engine":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_Computing_Engine
    - text: ", one of the first designs for a stored-program computer. In 1948, Turing joined"
    - link "Max Newman":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Newman
    - text: "'s"
    - link "Computing Machine Laboratory":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machine_Laboratory
    - text: at the
    - link "University of Manchester":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester
    - text: ", where he contributed to the development of early"
    - link "Manchester computers":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_computers
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-5-14"
    - text: and became interested in
    - link "mathematical biology":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_biology
    - text: . Turing wrote on the chemical basis of
    - link "morphogenesis":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphogenesis
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Milinkovitch-15"
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-googlescholar-3"
    - text: and predicted
    - link "oscillating chemical reactions":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_oscillator
    - text: such as the
    - link "Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belousov–Zhabotinsky_reaction
    - text: ", first observed in the 1960s. Despite these accomplishments, he was never fully recognised during his lifetime because much of his work was covered by the"
    - link "Official Secrets Act":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Secrets_Act_1939
    - text: .
    - superscript:
      - link "[15]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-6-16"
  - paragraph:
    - text: In 1952, Turing was prosecuted for
    - link "homosexual acts":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_indecency
    - text: . He accepted hormone treatment, a procedure commonly referred to as
    - link "chemical castration":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_castration
    - text: ", as an alternative to prison. Turing died on 7 June 1954, aged 41, from"
    - link "cyanide poisoning":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanide_poisoning
    - text: . An inquest determined his death as suicide, but the evidence is also consistent with accidental poisoning.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Copeland-1"
    - text: Following a campaign in 2009, British prime minister
    - link "Gordon Brown":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown
    - text: made an
    - link "official public apology":
      - /url: "#Government_apology_and_pardon"
    - text: for "the appalling way [Turing] was treated".
    - link "Queen Elizabeth II":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II
    - text: granted a
    - link "pardon":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_prerogative_of_mercy
    - text: in 2013. The term "
    - link "Alan Turing law":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing_law
    - text: "\" is used informally to refer to a 2017 law in the UK that retroactively pardoned men cautioned or convicted under historical legislation that outlawed homosexual acts."
    - superscript:
      - link "[16]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-BBC-pardon-17"
  - paragraph:
    - text: Turing left
    - link "an extensive legacy":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_of_Alan_Turing
    - text: in mathematics and computing which has become widely recognised with statues and
    - link "many things named after him":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_things_named_after_Alan_Turing
    - text: ", including"
    - link "an annual award":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_Award
    - text: for computing innovation. His portrait appears on the
    - link "Bank of England £50 note":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England_£50_note
    - text: ", first released on 23 June 2021 to coincide with his birthday. The audience vote in a"
    - link "2019 BBC series":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icons:_The_Greatest_Person_of_the_20th_Century
    - text: named Turing the greatest scientist of the 20th century.
    - superscript:
      - link "[17]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-7-18"
  - paragraph:
    - text: The cognitive scientist
    - link "Douglas Hofstadter":
      - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Hofstadter
    - text: "writes:"
    - superscript:
      - link "[18]":
        - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges1983xiii-19"
  - blockquote:
    - paragraph: Atheist, homosexual, eccentric, marathon-running mathematician, A. M. Turing was in large part responsible not only for the concept of computers, incisive theorems about their powers, and a clear vision of the possibility of computer minds, but also for the cracking of German ciphers during the Second World War. It is fair to say we owe much to Alan Turing for the fact that we are not under Nazi rule today.

      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing was born in
        - link "Maida Vale":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maida_Vale
        - text: ", London, while his father, Julius Mathison Turing, was on leave from his position with the"
        - link "Indian Civil Service":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Civil_Service
        - text: (ICS) of the
        - link "British Raj government":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj
        - text: at
        - link "Chatrapur":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatrapur
        - text: ", then in the"
        - link "Madras Presidency":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madras_Presidency
        - text: and presently in
        - link "Odisha":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odisha
        - text: state, in India.
        - superscript:
          - link "[19]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges19835-20"
        - superscript:
          - link "[20]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-8-21"
        - text: Turing's father was the son of a clergyman, the Rev. John Robert Turing, from a Scottish family of merchants that had been based in the Netherlands and included a
        - link "baronet":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baronet
        - text: . Turing's mother, Julius's wife, was Ethel Sara Turing (née Stoney), daughter of
        - link "Edward Waller Stoney":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Waller_Stoney
        - text: ", chief engineer of the"
        - link "Madras Railways":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madras_and_Southern_Mahratta_Railway
        - text: . The Stoneys were a
        - link "Protestant":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism_in_Ireland
        - link "Anglo-Irish":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Irish_people
        - link "gentry":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentry
        - text: family from both
        - link "County Tipperary":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Tipperary
        - text: and
        - link "County Longford":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Longford
        - text: ", while Ethel herself had spent much of her childhood in"
        - link "County Clare":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Clare
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[21]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-9-22"
        - text: Julius and Ethel married on 1 October 1907 at the Church of Ireland
        - link "St. Bartholomew's Church":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bartholomew's_Church,_Dublin
        - text: "on"
        - link "Clyde Road":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Road
        - text: in
        - link "Ballsbridge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballsbridge
        - text: ", Dublin."
        - superscript:
          - link "[22]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-10-23"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Julius's work with the ICS brought the family to British India, where his grandfather had been a general in the
        - link "Bengal Army":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Army
        - text: . However, both Julius and Ethel wanted their children to be brought up in Britain, so they moved to
        - link "Maida Vale":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maida_Vale
        - text: ","
        - superscript:
          - link "[23]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-englishheritaget-24"
        - text: London, where Alan Turing was born on 23 June 1912, as recorded by a
        - link "blue plaque":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaque
        - text: on the outside of the nursing home where he was born,
        - superscript:
          - link "[24]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-nature_20110316_the-25"
        - superscript:
          - link "[25]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-11-26"
        - text: which later became the
        - link "Colonnade Hotel":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade_Hotel_(London)
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[19]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges19835-20"
        - superscript:
          - link "[26]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-turingorguk-27"
        - text: Turing had an elder brother, John Ferrier Turing, father of
        - link "Dermot Turing":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dermot_Turing
        - text: ", 12th Baronet of the"
        - link "Turing baronets":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_baronets
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[27]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-12-28"
        - text: In 1922, he discovered Natural Wonders Every Child Should Know by
        - link "Edwin Tenney Brewster":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Tenney_Brewster
        - text: . He credited it with opening his eyes to science.
        - superscript:
          - link "[28]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198316-29"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing's father's civil service commission was still active during Turing's childhood years, and his parents travelled between
        - link "Hastings":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings
        - text: in the United Kingdom
        - superscript:
          - link "[29]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges19836-30"
        - text: and India, leaving their two sons to stay with a retired
        - link "Army":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army
        - text: couple. At Hastings, Turing stayed at
        - link "Baston Lodge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baston_Lodge
        - text: ", Upper Maze Hill,"
        - link "St Leonards-on-Sea":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Leonards-on-Sea
        - text: ", now marked with a blue plaque."
        - superscript:
          - link "[30]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Hastings_&_St._Leonards_Observer_-_29_June_2012_-_Plaque_unveiled_at_Turing's_home_in_St_Leonards-31"
        - text: The plaque was unveiled on 23 June 2012, the centenary of Turing's birth.
        - superscript:
          - link "[31]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-BBC_News_-_25_June_2012_-_St_Leonards_plaque_marks_Alan_Turing's_early_years-32"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Very early in life, Turing's parents purchased a house in
        - link "Guildford":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildford
        - text: in 1927, and Turing lived there during school holidays. The location is also marked with a blue plaque.
        - superscript:
          - link "[32]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-guildford-dragon_20121129_founder-33"
    - region "School":
      - heading "School" [level=3]
      - figure "Turing at age 16, c. 1928 – c. 1929":
        - link:
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alan_Turing_Aged_16.jpg
          - img
        - text: Turing at age 16, c. 1928 – c. 1929
      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing's parents enrolled him at St Michael's, a primary school at 20 Charles Road,
        - link "St Leonards-on-Sea":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Leonards-on-Sea
        - text: ", from the age of six to nine. The headmistress recognised his talent, noting that she \"...had clever boys and hardworking boys, but Alan is a genius\"."
        - superscript:
          - link "[33]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-13-34"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Between January 1922 and 1926, Turing was educated at Hazelhurst Preparatory School, an independent school in the village of
        - link "Frant":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frant
        - text: in Sussex (now
        - link "East Sussex":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Sussex
        - text: ).
        - superscript:
          - link "[34]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-14-35"
        - text: In 1926, at the age of 13, he went on to
        - link "Sherborne School":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherborne_School
        - text: ","
        - superscript:
          - link "[35]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-15-36"
        - text: an independent boarding school in the market town of
        - link "Sherborne":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherborne
        - text: in Dorset, where he boarded at Westcott House. The first day of term coincided with the
        - link "1926 General Strike":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1926_United_Kingdom_general_strike
        - text: ", in Britain, but Turing was so determined to attend that he rode his bicycle unaccompanied 60 miles (97 km) from"
        - link "Southampton":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton
        - text: to Sherborne, stopping overnight at an inn.
        - superscript:
          - link "[36]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-metamagical-37"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing's natural inclination towards mathematics and science did not earn him respect from some of the teachers at Sherborne, whose
        - link "definition of education":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definition_of_education
        - text: placed more emphasis on the
        - link "classics":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classics
        - text: ". His headmaster wrote to his parents: \"I hope he will not fall between two stools. If he is to stay at public school, he must aim at becoming educated. If he is to be solely a Scientific Specialist, he is wasting his time at a public school\"."
        - superscript:
          - link "[28]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198316-29"
        - text: Despite this, Turing continued to show remarkable ability in the studies he loved, solving advanced problems in 1927 without having studied even elementary
        - link "calculus":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus
        - text: . In 1928, aged 16, Turing encountered
        - link "Albert Einstein":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein
        - text: "'s work; not only did he grasp it, but it is possible that he managed to deduce Einstein's questioning of"
        - link "Newton's laws of motion":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton's_laws_of_motion
        - text: from a text in which this was never made explicit.
        - superscript:
          - link "[37]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198334-38"
      - 'figure "Turing (seated second from left) in Cornwall, with fellow Shirburnians: Edwin Davis, John Bennett, Peter White, Peter Hogg (seated second from right), and Duncan Carse, in April 1930."':
        - link:
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alan_Turing_in_Cornwall_April_1930_with_Peter_Hogg,_Edwin_Davis,_John_Bennett,_Peter_White,_and_Duncan_Carse.jpg
          - img
        - text: Turing (seated second from left) in
        - link "Cornwall":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall
        - text: ", with fellow Shirburnians: Edwin Davis, John Bennett, Peter White,"
        - link "Peter Hogg":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Hogg_(Shiburnian)
        - text: (seated second from right), and Duncan Carse, in April 1930.
    - region "Christopher Morcom":
      - heading "Christopher Morcom" [level=3]
      - note:
        - text: "Main article:"
        - link "Christopher Morcom":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Morcom
      - paragraph:
        - text: At Sherborne, Turing formed a significant friendship with fellow pupil Christopher Collan Morcom (13 July 1911 – 13 February 1930),
        - superscript:
          - link "[38]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-16-39"
        - text: who has been described as Turing's first love.
        - superscript:
          - link "[39]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-17-40"
        - superscript:
          - link "[40]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-18-41"
        - superscript:
          - link "[41]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-19-42"
        - text: Morcom was a student athlete, photographer, music collector,
        - superscript:
          - link "[42]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-cm-43"
        - superscript:
          - link "[43]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges201243,_47-44"
        - text: and astronomer, notable for
        - link "his elaborate school pranks":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Morcom#Sense_of_humour
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[44]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges201256-45"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Their relationship, particularly in discussion of science and astronomy, is collected in letters. The Enigma details how Morcom "used to tease Alan a good deal", with various running
        - link "in-jokes":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-joke
        - text: and pranks to inconvenience Turing.
        - superscript:
          - link "[45]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges201255-46"
        - text: Nevertheless, their intellectual correspondences provided inspiration in Turing's future endeavours.
      - paragraph:
        - text: In February 1930, shortly before graduation, their relationship was cut short by Morcom's death. Months prior, the two had had a weeklong tour of
        - link "Trinity College, Cambridge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge
        - text: to sit
        - link "scholarship":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship
        - text: examinations.
        - superscript:
          - link "[46]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges201254–55-47"
        - text: Days after attending a
        - link "Salisbury Singers":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Singers
        - text: concert, Morcom died of complications of
        - link "bovine tuberculosis":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bovine_tuberculosis
        - text: ", which he had contracted earlier in life."
        - superscript:
          - link "[47]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-NYReviewBooks-48"
        - superscript:
          - link "[48]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-20-49"
        - superscript:
          - link "[49]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-teuscher-50"
      - paragraph: "Morcom's death caused Turing great sorrow. He accepted multiple prizes on Morcom's behalf, choosing books in Morcom's memory as prizes; and Turing also won the posthumous Christopher Morcom Science Prize, organized by Morcom's mother. In a letter to Morcom's mother, Frances Isobel Morcom (née Swan), Turing wrote:"
      - blockquote:
        - paragraph:
          - text: I am sure I could not have found anywhere another companion so brilliant and yet so charming and unconceited. I regarded my interest in my work, and in such things as astronomy (to which he introduced me) as something to be shared with him and I think he felt a little the same about me ... I know I must put as much energy if not as much interest into my work as if he were alive, because that is what he would like me to do.
          - superscript:
            - link "[50]":
              - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198361-51"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing's relationship with Morcom's mother continued long after Morcom's death, with her sending gifts to Turing, and him sending letters, typically on Morcom's birthday.
        - superscript:
          - link "[51]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198387-52"
        - text: "A day before the third anniversary of Morcom's death (13 February 1933), he wrote to Mrs. Morcom:"
      - blockquote:
        - paragraph:
          - text: I expect you will be thinking of Chris when this reaches you. I shall too, and this letter is just to tell you that I shall be thinking of Chris and of you tomorrow. I am sure that he is as happy now as he was when he was here. Your affectionate Alan.
          - superscript:
            - link "[52]":
              - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198390-53"
      - paragraph:
        - text: It has been speculated that Morcom's death was the cause of Turing's
        - link "atheism":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheism
        - text: and "the conviction that all phenomena must have
        - link "materialistic":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materialism
        - text: explanations".
        - superscript:
          - link "[53]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-time_990624-54"
        - text: "Circa 1932, Turing wrote The Nature of Spirit while visiting Morcom's family home. His writings show a belief in such concepts as a spirit surviving death independent of the body. In a later letter, also written to Morcom's mother, Turing wrote:"
      - blockquote:
        - paragraph:
          - text: Personally, I believe that spirit is really eternally connected with matter but certainly not by the same kind of body ... as regards the actual connection between spirit and body I consider that the body can hold on to a 'spirit', whilst the body is alive and awake the two are firmly connected. When the body is asleep I cannot guess what happens but when the body dies, the 'mechanism' of the body, holding the spirit is gone and the spirit finds a new body sooner or later, perhaps immediately.
          - superscript:
            - link "[54]":
              - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198382-83-55"
          - superscript:
            - link "[55]":
              - /url: "#cite_note-oldshirburnian_20200815-56"
    - region "University and work on computability":
      - heading "University and work on computability" [level=3]
      - figure "Turing in the 1930s":
        - link:
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alan_Turing_az_1930-as_években.jpg
          - img
        - text: Turing in the 1930s
      - paragraph:
        - text: In 1929 Turing and his friend
        - link "Christopher Morcom":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Morcom
        - text: applied for scholarships at
        - link "Trinity College, Cambridge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge
        - text: . Morcom, who was successful, had various advantages over Turing – he was nearly a year older, and both his father and brother had studied at Trinity. However, he died three months after the offer was made. Turing, on the other hand, was unsuccessful, but sat the
        - link "King's College, Cambridge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College,_Cambridge
        - text: Scholarship Examination in Mathematics in 1930. King's reserved most of its places for
        - link "Etonians":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etonians
        - text: (there was a historic link with Eton as a feeder institution), making the exam very competitive for candidates from other schools. However, its examiners had a slightly different slant to those in other colleges.
        - superscript:
          - link "[56]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198357,_58-57"
        - text: Hodges describes the King's examiners as looking for "a spark of originality" and notes that the papers were "notorious for their unorthodox questions".
      - paragraph:
        - text: Turing was awarded an
        - link "exhibition":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_(scholarship)
        - text: (a lower-value scholarship) worth £80 per annum (equivalent to about £4,300 as of 2023).
        - superscript:
          - link "[57]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges198374–75-58"
        - superscript:
          - link "[58]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-21-59"
        - text: His undergraduate studies at Cambridge were from February 1931 to November 1934. He studied "Schedule B" of the
        - link "Mathematical Tripos":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_Tripos
        - text: course.
        - superscript:
          - link "[59]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-22-60"
        - text: He was awarded first-class honours in mathematics. His dissertation, On the Gaussian error function, written during his senior year and delivered in November 1934 proved a version of the
        - link "central limit theorem":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_limit_theorem
        - text: . It was finally accepted on 16 March 1935. By spring of that same year, Turing started his master's course (
        - link "Part III":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part_III_of_the_Mathematical_Tripos
        - text: )—which he completed in 1937—and, at the same time, he published his first paper, a one-page article called Equivalence of left and right almost periodicity (sent on 23 April), featured in the tenth volume of the
        - link "Journal of the London Mathematical Society":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Mathematical_Society
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[60]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-23-61"
        - text: Later that year, Turing was elected a
        - link "Fellow":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow
        - text: of King's College on the strength of his dissertation
        - superscript:
          - link "[61]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-24-62"
        - text: where he served as a lecturer.
        - superscript:
          - link "[62]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-lecturer-63"
        - text: However, unknown to Turing, the version of the theorem he proved in his paper had already been proven by
        - link "Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarl_Waldemar_Lindeberg
        - text: in 1922. Despite this, the committee found Turing's methods original and so regarded the work worthy of consideration for the fellowship.
        - link "Abram Besicovitch":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abram_Besicovitch
        - text: "'s report for the committee went so far as to say that if Turing's work had been published before Lindeberg's, it would have been \"an important event in the mathematical literature of that year\"."
        - superscript:
          - link "[63]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-25-64"
        - superscript:
          - link "[64]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges1983113-65"
        - superscript:
          - link "[65]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-26-66"
      - paragraph:
        - text: Between the springs of 1935 and 1936, at the same time as
        - link "Alonzo Church":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Church
        - text: ", Turing worked on the decidability of problems, starting from"
        - link "Gödel's incompleteness theorems":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gödel's_incompleteness_theorems
        - text: . In mid-April 1936, Turing sent
        - link "Max Newman":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Newman
        - text: the first draft typescript of his investigations. That same month, Church published his An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory, with similar conclusions to Turing's then-yet unpublished work. Finally, on 28 May of that year, he finished and delivered his 36-page paper for publication called "
        - link "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Computable_Numbers,_with_an_Application_to_the_Entscheidungsproblem
        - text: "\"."
        - superscript:
          - link "[66]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-computable-67"
        - superscript:
          - link "[67]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-27-68"
        - text: It was published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society journal in two parts, the first on 30 November and the second on 23 December.
        - superscript:
          - link "[68]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-28-69"
        - text: In this paper, Turing proved results on the limits of computation, introducing the formal and simple hypothetical devices that became known as
        - link "Turing machines":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_machine
        - text: . The
        - link "Entscheidungsproblem":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entscheidungsproblem
        - text: (decision problem) was originally posed by German mathematician
        - link "David Hilbert":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert
        - text: in 1928, and consists of seeking a computational procedure for proving or disproving theorems in the logical calculus employed by Hilbert. Turing argued that his "computing machine" would be capable of performing any conceivable mathematical computation if it were representable by finitary means (as an
        - link "algorithm":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm
        - text: ). He went on to prove that there was no solution to the decision problem by first showing that some variants of the
        - link "halting problem":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem
        - text: for Turing machines are
        - link "undecidable":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_problem
        - text: ": in parcitular, it is not possible to decide algorithmically whether a Turing machine will produce an infinite output. This paper has been called \"easily the most influential math paper in history\"."
        - superscript:
          - link "[69]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-29-70"
      - figure "King's College, Cambridge, where Turing was an undergraduate in 1931 and became a Fellow in 1935. The computer room is named after him.":
        - link:
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20130808_Kings_College_Front_Court_Fountain_Crop_03.jpg
          - img
        - link "King's College, Cambridge":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College,_Cambridge
        - text: ", where Turing was an undergraduate in 1931 and became a Fellow in 1935. The computer room is named after him."
      - paragraph:
        - text: Although
        - link "Turing's proof":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing's_proof
        - text: was published shortly after Church's equivalent proof using his
        - link "lambda calculus":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus
        - text: ","
        - superscript:
          - link "[70]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-30-71"
        - text: Turing's approach is considerably more accessible and intuitive than Church's.
        - superscript:
          - link "[71]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-31-72"
        - text: It also included a notion of a 'Universal Machine' (now known as a
        - link "universal Turing machine":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Turing_machine
        - text: ), with the idea that such a machine could perform the tasks of any other computation machine (as indeed could Church's lambda calculus). According to the
        - link "Church–Turing thesis":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church–Turing_thesis
        - text: ", Turing machines and the lambda calculus are capable of computing anything that is computable."
        - link "John von Neumann":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_von_Neumann
        - text: acknowledged that the central concept of the modern computer was due to Turing's paper.
        - superscript:
          - link "[72]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-32-73"
        - text: To this day, Turing machines are a central object of study in
        - link "theory of computation":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_computation
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[73]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-33-74"
      - paragraph:
        - text: From September 1936 to July 1938, Turing spent most of his time studying under Church at
        - link "Princeton University":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University
        - text: ","
        - superscript:
          - link "[5]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-bowen19-6"
        - text: in the second year as a
        - link "Jane Eliza Procter Visiting Fellow":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Eliza_Procter_Fellowship
        - text: . In addition to his purely mathematical work, he studied cryptology and also built three of four stages of an electro-mechanical
        - link "binary multiplier":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_multiplier
        - text: .
        - superscript:
          - link "[74]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges1983138-75"
        - text: In June 1938, he obtained his PhD from the
        - link "Department of Mathematics":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University_Department_of_Mathematics
        - text: at Princeton;
        - superscript:
          - text: "["
          - link "citation needed":
            - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
          - text: "]"
        - text: his dissertation,
        - link "Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_of_Logic_Based_on_Ordinals
        - text: ","
        - superscript:
          - link "[75]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-turing_thesis_actual-76"
        - superscript:
          - link "[76]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-35-77"
        - text: introduced the concept of
        - link "ordinal logic":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_logic
        - text: and the notion of
        - link "relative computing":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_reduction
        - text: ", in which Turing machines are augmented with so-called"
        - link "oracles":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_machine
        - text: ", allowing the study of problems that cannot be solved by Turing machines. Von Neumann wanted to hire him as his"
        - link "postdoctoral assistant":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postdoctoral_researcher
        - text: ", but he went back to the United Kingdom."
        - superscript:
          - link "[77]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-36-78"
        - text: His thesis was republished in the journal Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society in 1939,
        - superscript:
          - link "[78]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-turing_thesis_journal-79"
  - region "Career and research":
    - heading "Career and research" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: When Turing returned to Cambridge, he attended lectures given in 1939 by
      - link "Ludwig Wittgenstein":
        - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Wittgenstein
      - text: about the
      - link "foundations of mathematics":
        - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundations_of_mathematics
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[79]":
          - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges1983152-80"
      - text: The lectures have been reconstructed verbatim, including interjections from Turing and other students, from students' notes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[80]":
          - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-37-81"
      - text: Turing and Wittgenstein argued and disagreed, with Turing defending
      - link "formalism":
        - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy_of_mathematics#Formalism
      - text: and Wittgenstein propounding his view that mathematics does not discover any absolute truths, but rather invents them.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHodges1983153-154-82"
    - region "Cryptanalysis":
      - heading "Cryptanalysis" [level=3]
      - paragraph:
        - text: During the Second World War, Turing was a leading participant in the breaking of German ciphers at
        - link "Bletchley Park":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bletchley_Park
        - text: . The historian and wartime codebreaker
        - link "Asa Briggs":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asa_Briggs
        - text: has said, "You needed exceptional talent, you needed genius at Bletchley and Turing's was that genius."
        - superscript:
          - link "[82]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-38-83"
      - paragraph:
        - text: From September 1938, Turing worked part-time with the
        - link "Government Code and Cypher School":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Code_and_Cypher_School
        - text: (GC&CS), the British codebreaking organisation. He concentrated on
        - link "cryptanalysis of the Enigma cipher machine":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis_of_the_Enigma
        - text: used by
        - link "Nazi Germany":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany
        - text: ", together with"
        - link "Dilly Knox":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilly_Knox
        - text: ", a senior GC&CS codebreaker."
        - superscript:
          - link "[83]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-39-84"
        - text: Soon after the July 1939 meeting near
        - link "Warsaw":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw
        - text: at which the
        - link "Polish Cipher Bureau":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Cipher_Bureau
        - text: gave the British and French details of the wiring of
        - link "Enigma machine's rotors":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_rotor_details
        - text: and their method of decrypting
        - link "Enigma machine":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_machine
        - text: "'s messages, Turing and Knox developed a broader solution."
        - superscript:
          - link "[84]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-Auto6D-40-85"
        - text: The Polish method relied on an insecure
        - link "indicator":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis#Indicator
        - text: procedure that the Germans were likely to change, which they in fact did in May 1940. Turing's approach was more general, using
        - link "crib-based decryption":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis_of_the_Enigma#Crib-based_decryption
        - text: for which he produced the functional specification of the
        - link "bombe":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombe
        - text: (an improvement on the Polish
        - link "Bomba":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomba_(cryptography)
        - text: ).
        - superscript:
          - link "[85]":
            - /url: "#cite_note-wired_20120618_turing-86"
      - figure "Two cottages in the stable yard at Bletchley Park. Turing worked here in 1939 and 1940, before moving to Hut 8.":
        - link:
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Turing_flat.jpg
          - img
        - text: Two cottages in the stable yard at
        - link "Bletchley Park":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bletchley_Park
        - text: . Turing worked here in 1939 and 1940, before moving to
        - link "Hut 8":
          - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hut_8
        - text: .
      - paragraph:
        - text: On 4 September 1939, the day after the UK declared war on Germany, Turing reported to Bletchley Park, the wartime station of GC&CS.

          - link "[86]":
            - /url: "#cite_note
